extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers interested in media hoaxes and media history
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic description and analysis of a specific 19th-century journalistic/media hoax (the "Global Warming Hoax of 1874"), its content, its veracity, reception, and related examples. Useful for understanding features and verification of media hoaxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic/media hoax (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A journalistic/media hoax is "a fictitious story purposefully written to appear as real and factual."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explicitly defines the Global Warming Hoax of 1874 as a journalistic/media hoax and uses that label to classify the piece; this definition is the primary evaluative standard for the article's veracity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fabricated sensational scientific claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The hoax's column ('A Scientific Sensation') claimed that astronomer Giovanni Donati discovered that the transatlantic telegraph cable was causing the Earth to be pulled towards the Sun and warned that in twelve years there would be a dramatic increase in temperature causing the extinction of all life on Earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensational, extraordinary scientific claims (apocalyptic timelines, dramatic physical mechanisms) are characteristic techniques used to create a hoax's apparent newsworthiness and urgency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anecdotal/unverified sourcing (friend's letter, single correspondent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The column states Legendre's friend, who was in Italy at the time, wrote to Legendre to inform him of Donati's discovery; the narrative relies on this personal letter as its primary source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on a single anecdotal or unverifiable source (a 'friend' or private correspondence) is a common marker that the piece may not be factual; such sourcing should prompt verification against independent records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing real people/events with false causal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The hoax uses real historical elements—Giovanni Donati (a real astronomer) and the transatlantic telegraph cable—but assigns false causes and consequences (e.g., telegraph cable altering Earth's orbit; Donati dying from stress caused by this).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoaxes often combine accurate factual anchors with fabricated causal links; presence of real names/events does not guarantee accuracy and may be used to lend false plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent scientific detail used without community corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece reports Donati had been 'calculating and recording the location of the Earth in orbit' and claimed measurable changes after the cable was laid, yet the article notes Donati 'was not universally credited by his scientific colleagues.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical or scientific-sounding measurements and apparatus are frequently invoked in hoaxes; the absence of corroboration from the relevant scientific community (or claims of lack of credit) is a warning sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative of intervention and reversal to increase drama
rubrics_metrics.description: The hoax recounts that Donati organized an expedition to cut the cable, observed the distance returned to normal, and then that the repaired cable caused the problem to recur, culminating in Donati's illness and death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoaxes often add dramatic, causal episodes (heroic interventions, observable reversals) to make the story coherent and compelling; these episodes should be fact-checked against primary sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality-check / verification criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Reality' section contrasts the article's claims with historical facts: Giovanni Donati was real but died of cholera in 1873 (not from stress of Earth's motion), and the claim about causing the first break in the transatlantic cable is false because the first break actually occurred in 1858.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification involves checking: biographical records (dates and causes of death), timelines of events (dates of cable breaks), and primary sources. Discrepancies between claimed causes/effects and documented historical facts indicate fabrication or exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception and propagation as indicators of impact
rubrics_metrics.description: The article was published in a few other newspapers but 'failed to gain much traction.' Hoaxes in the 19th century were becoming more common, sometimes prompting jokes or commentary in other papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How widely and how credibly a story is reprinted or discussed can indicate its short-term impact but not its veracity; ephemeral or jokey reception (satirical responses, chuckles) may signal contemporaneous skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual criterion: prevalence and form of 19th-century hoaxes
rubrics_metrics.description: The page situates the item among many 19th-century journalistic/media hoaxes (e.g., Great Wall of China hoax, The Balloon-Hoax, The Great Moon Hoax), noting these were common as media expanded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the historical media environment (rise of newspapers, common hoax formats) helps evaluate why such a piece could be published and how readers of the time might have perceived it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cataloging similar hoaxes as comparative evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The article lists similar incidents—Great Wall of China hoax; The Balloon-Hoax; The Bathtub Hoax; The Man Eating Tree of Madagascar; The Great Moon Hoax; The Central Park Zoo Escape—as comparable journalistic/media hoaxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparing a suspect story to known hoax patterns and specific historical examples can aid in classification and in identifying recurring rhetorical or structural tactics used by hoaxers.
